the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders is essential to the overall management of HIV disease and that psychopharmacotherapy is a critical component of this treatment.

there are no definitive data to support any specific antidepressant or antipsychotic as a first choice in the treatment of depression or psychosis in HIV-infected individuals; rather, the choice of treatment should be based on the patient's clinical presentation and the side effect profile of the medication.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are a growing number of controlled studies that have begun to address the efficacy and tolerability of antidepressant medications in HIV-infected patients.
HIV infection is a neuropsychiatric disorder that is frequently associated with other neuropsychiatric syndromes.
the use of antidepressants and other psychotropic agents is a reasonable and safe approach for treating neuropsychiatric disorders associated with immunodeficiency.
The main takeaway from our work is that

HIV-infected persons should not be denied treatment with antidepressants, antipsychotics, and other psychotropic agents because of the presence of immunodeficiency, and the use of these agents should not be withheld because of the presence or absence of immunodeficiency.

HIV infection should not be considered as an exclusion criterion for the diagnosis of psychiatric disorders and that psychotropic medications should be considered as a first-line treatment option for HIV-infected individuals suffering from psychiatric disorders.
the use of antidepressants is safe and can be efficacious in the context of HIV disease.
